question: After a distal femur fracture, a patient has a dorsalis pedis pulse but reports severe pain on passive extension of the toes and a tense anterior compartment. The measured compartment pressure is 35 mmHg; systolic BP is 100 mmHg, diastolic 65 mmHg. Which statement is MOST accurate?

answers.text: The presence of a pulse excludes compartment syndrome; reassure and discharge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A palpable pulse does NOT exclude compartment syndrome. Pulses are lost only when compartment pressure exceeds systolic BP — well after irreversible ischaemia has begun.

answers.text: ΔP is 30 mmHg (borderline); monitor closely in ICU for 2 hours before deciding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. ΔP = 65 − 35 = 30 mmHg, which is exactly at the threshold. Combined with clinical signs (pain on passive stretch, tense compartment), fasciotomy should not be delayed.

answers.text: Clinical signs plus ΔP ≤ 30 mmHg mandate immediate four-compartment fasciotomy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When clinical signs of compartment syndrome are present AND ΔP ≤ 30 mmHg, fasciotomy must not be delayed. Pulse presence is irrelevant to this decision.

answers.text: Intravenous morphine and splint removal are sufficient initial treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Removing constrictive dressings is a first step, but if compartment pressures reach the threshold, surgical fasciotomy is mandatory and must not be replaced by analgesia alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: Critical point: the 6 Ps of compartment syndrome include pain and paraesthesia — both occur before pulse loss. ΔP ≤ 30 mmHg is the fasciotomy threshold regardless of pulse status.
Excellent. Key principle: a present pulse does NOT exclude compartment syndrome. The clinical triad (pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, paresthesia) + ΔP ≤ 30 mmHg = fasciotomy now.
